Vignette: Daniel Tran, Age 31

Daniel grew up in a coastal province in Vietnam, where typhoons were a fact of life - something people prepared for, endured, and moved past. He had lived through storms before. But nothing in his experience had prepared him for what happened three years ago, when a category-five typhoon made landfall while he was visiting his parents' home during a national holiday. The storm surge came faster than anyone anticipated. Within minutes, the ground floor of his childhood home was submerged. Daniel remembers standing on a chair in the dark, holding his elderly mother above the waterline for nearly four hours, listening to the walls groan and feeling the floor shift beneath him. His father did not survive. He was found the following morning, two streets away.

Daniel returned to his work as a judge in Ho Chi Minh City within two weeks. He told himself this was the right thing to do - that the courts needed him, that staying busy was a form of respect for his father, who had always admired his career. In the early months, this seemed to work. He was thorough, composed, and well-regarded by colleagues who had no idea what had happened. But at night, the water came back. He would wake at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, sheets soaked through, certain that the floor was moving beneath him. His wife, Linh, would reach for him in the dark, and he would lie still, not wanting to alarm her, staring at the ceiling until dawn.

Over time, the intrusions began finding their way into his waking hours. Sitting on the bench, he sometimes hears the sound of rushing water when the courtroom is completely silent. Heavy rainfall - even the sound of it against the courthouse windows - can pull him out of the present entirely. He has learned to keep a glass of water on his desk and to fix his eyes on it when he feels himself beginning to drift, using it as an anchor. His clerks have noticed that he sometimes pauses mid-sentence and takes a long, deliberate breath before continuing. They assume it is a judicial affectation. He does not correct them.

Daniel has become meticulous about control in ways he did not used to be. He checks weather forecasts obsessively before leaving home, plans alternate routes that avoid underpasses, and has quietly arranged for his apartment to be on the highest floor available. He no longer visits his mother in the province, offering instead to fly her to the city, and the guilt of this sits heavily with him. He loves her. He cannot go back.

At home, Linh tells him gently that he has become distant. He agrees with her, which seems to frustrate her more than if he had argued. He finds it difficult to feel much of anything in the evenings - a flatness that descends after work and does not lift. He goes through the motions of dinner, conversation, the small rituals of their marriage, but describes it to himself as watching his own life from slightly outside his body. There are moments, usually early in the morning before full consciousness sets in, when he feels something close to warmth. But they pass quickly.

What troubles Daniel most - what finally prompted him to seek help - is a growing fear about his work. He is a man whose entire professional identity rests on his capacity for clear, dispassionate judgment. He believes in the law's ability to impose order on chaos. But lately he has begun to wonder whether he can trust his own mind. Whether the man who sits on that bench, composed and certain, is the same man who wakes in the dark convinced that the floor is giving way. He has not told anyone at the court. He is not sure he can afford to.
